title: HOLY DOESN’T MEAN SEXLESS: WHAT SONG OF SOLOMON REVEALS ABOUT DESIRE
paragraphs:
HOLY DOESN’T MEAN SEXLESS: WHAT SONG OF SOLOMON REVEALS ABOUT DESIRE
The Bible contains a love song so intimate that generations of believers have struggled to know what to do with it. Maybe the problem was never that God spoke too openly about desire. Maybe the problem was that we confused holiness with pretending desire doesn’t exist.
There is a book in your Bible that sounds almost dangerous when read slowly.
Not because it is sinful.
Because it is honest.
A woman longs for a man.
A man delights in a woman.
They notice each other.
They miss each other.
They search for each other.
They speak openly about beauty, attraction, longing, exclusivity, bodies, kisses, fragrance, gardens, touch, desire, and love.
And somehow...
God allowed all of it into Scripture.
Maybe that makes you uncomfortable.
Maybe nobody in church ever told you what to do with the Song of Songs.

Maybe you were taught that being holy meant becoming strangely disconnected from your own humanity. That if you loved Jesus enough, attraction would stop being powerful. Desire would become embarrassing. Your body would become something spiritual people tolerated rather than something the Creator deliberately made.
So when desire awakened in you, you felt dirty before you had even done anything wrong.
When you noticed someone's beauty, guilt arrived before wisdom could.
When your body wanted what your convictions told you to wait for, you assumed the struggle itself meant you were failing God.
And perhaps nobody ever told you this:
Desire is not the same thing as sin.
That distinction could change the way some Christians see themselves.
Because the Bible does not begin with embarrassed bodies.
It begins with God.
Then creation.
Then a man.
Then a woman.
Then this astonishing declaration:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Read that again.
Naked.
Together.
Unashamed.
Before lust corrupted desire...
before adultery betrayed covenant...
before pornography commercialized bodies...
before abuse weaponized sexuality...
before people learned to use one another...
there was nakedness without shame.
Human sexuality did not crawl out of hell.
God created human beings embodied and sexual before Genesis 3 ever happened.
Sin did not invent sexuality.
Sin distorted it.
And that difference matters enormously.

Because Christianity is not a religion in which the body is inherently evil and the spirit is inherently good. Scripture says God created humanity male and female in His image. The body belongs to God's good creation. And Christianity reaches its astonishing climax not with humanity escaping embodiment forever, but with resurrection.
Then we arrive at one of Scripture's most surprising books.
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
Shir HaShirim.
The Song of Songs.
The Hebrew construction is a superlative—something like “the greatest song.”
And what is this great song singing about?
Desire.
Not cheap desire.
Not anonymous desire.
Not pornography.
Not adultery.
Not conquest.
Not using another human being as a narcotic for loneliness.
It sings of personal, embodied, delighted love between a man and a woman.
Listen to the woman's opening longing:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.

“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth...”
Song of Songs 1:2.
There it is.
In Scripture.
A kiss.
Wanted.
Desired.
Spoken by a woman who is not portrayed as spiritually defective because she longs to be kissed.
That alone may confront a distorted theology some Christians have carried for years.
The woman in the Song is not merely an object being desired.
She desires.
She speaks.
She seeks.
She celebrates.
She has a voice.
And the man does not speak about her as disposable flesh.
He delights in her.
He notices her.
He praises her.
Again and again, their desire is profoundly personal.
Not merely, “I want a body.”
But...
I want you.
That is where biblical desire begins separating itself from lust.
Lust depersonalizes.
Love recognizes.
Lust asks, “What can your body give me?”
Covenantal love asks, “How can I give myself faithfully to you?”
Lust consumes.
Love cherishes.
Lust can survive without knowing someone's soul.
Love wants the person.
This is why pornography is not simply “strong sexual desire.”
Pornography trains desire to consume images detached from covenant, responsibility, fidelity, sacrifice, and genuine knowledge of the person.
Jesus exposes lust at the level of the heart in Matthew 5:27–28.
But notice what He does not say.
He does not say beauty is evil.
He does not say marriage is dirty.
He does not say sexual union is inherently shameful.
He confronts desire that has become covetous—desire that reaches toward someone who is not yours to possess.
There is an enormous difference between experiencing attraction and choosing to cultivate lust.
Somebody needs that distinction tonight.
Because perhaps you have spent years condemning yourself for being human when Christ was calling you to become holy in your humanity.
Holiness is not the annihilation of desire.
Holiness is desire surrendered to God.
It is wanting something deeply without allowing that desire to become your master.
It is being able to say:
“Jesus, I want this. You already know I want this. But I want You more than I want what I want.”
That is not repression.
That is worship.
And Song of Songs contains another line our generation desperately needs:
“Do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.”
The warning appears repeatedly throughout the Song.
That is breathtakingly balanced.
The same Bible that celebrates desire also tells desire:
Wait.
There is a time.
There is an order.
There is wisdom.
There are boundaries.
Fire is beautiful in a fireplace.
The same fire tearing through the walls can destroy the house.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is where the fire burns.
And perhaps that explains some of your scars.
You were not wrong because you wanted love.
You were not wrong because you wanted to be held.
You were not wrong because you wanted intimacy.
You were not wrong because you wanted someone to look at you and choose you.
But maybe you tried to satisfy a holy hunger through an unholy shortcut.
Maybe you slept with someone because, for one night, being wanted felt almost like being loved.
Maybe you stayed in a relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ because loneliness terrified you more than compromise.
Maybe you kept returning to pornography because pixels never rejected you.
Maybe masturbation became less about pleasure and more about anesthesia.
Maybe flirtation became proof that you still mattered.
Maybe attention became your drug.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you're doing fine.
But you know what happens when the room gets quiet.
You remember.
And shame starts preaching.
“You're filthy.”
“You ruined yourself.”
“God must be disgusted with you.”
“No godly person would struggle like this.”
“You can never become clean again.”
But shame is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not walk toward sexually broken people with stones in His hands.
He came with truth sharp enough to expose sin and grace strong enough to rescue sinners.
That does not mean Jesus minimizes sexual sin.
He does something far more beautiful.
He forgives and transforms sinners.
The Gospel never says your sin does not matter.
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that your sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
There is a world of difference.
Grace is not Jesus pretending the stain isn't there.
Grace is Jesus doing what you could never do to remove your guilt before God.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The adulterer can repent.
The porn addict can repent.
The sexually compromised believer can repent.
The person who gave away what they wish they had guarded can repent.
The person carrying years of secret fantasy can repent.
The person who has made an idol of romance can repent.
The person who confused being desired with being valuable can repent.
And repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind, a turning.
Not merely:
“I feel horrible about myself.”
But:
“Jesus, I agree with You now. I don't want sin ruling me anymore. Turn me around.”
And this is where Christ becomes infinitely more beautiful than mere religious behavior modification.
Christianity does not say, “Clean yourself up sexually so Jesus might finally want you.”
Christianity announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
He moves toward sinners first.
Then grace teaches us to leave the darkness.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace retrains desire.
It teaches your eyes where to look.
Your hands what to refuse.
Your body whom it belongs to.
Your loneliness where to run.
Your sexuality where it belongs.
Your heart whom to worship.
Because the deepest problem with disordered desire is ultimately not that human beings desire too intensely.
Often, we desire created things as though they could do what only God can do.
We ask romance to save us.
Sex to validate us.
Marriage to complete us.
Beauty to give us worth.
Attention to convince us we matter.
Another body to silence the ache in our own soul.
But no husband can be your Savior.
No wife can be your Messiah.
No orgasm can resurrect a dead heart.
No human embrace can bear the infinite weight of your identity.
No amount of sexual attention can finally convince a soul that it is eternally loved.
That throne belongs to Jesus.
And when Christ occupies the throne, human love does not become less beautiful.
It becomes freer.
Now you can love someone without demanding that they become God for you.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can desire intimacy without sacrificing obedience to obtain it.
You can experience attraction without becoming enslaved to fantasy.
You can enjoy beauty without turning a person into an object.
You can be single without being incomplete.
You can be married without making your spouse responsible for healing every wound inside you.
And if you fall?
You run toward Christ.
Not away.
Because there is another fire burning through Song of Songs.
Near the end, the poetry reaches its summit:

שִׂימֵנִי כַחוֹתָם עַל־לִבֶּךָ
כַּחוֹתָם עַל־זְרוֹעֶךָ
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Simeni khachotam al-libbekha, kachotam al-zero'ekha, ki-azzah khammavet ahavah.

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death...”
Song of Songs 8:6.
Then comes an extraordinary Hebrew expression:
שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
shalhevetyah.
A blazing flame.

The ending -yah has traditionally led some translations and interpreters to render the expression as something like “a flame of Yah” or “a flame of the LORD,” while other translations understand it idiomatically as an intensely powerful flame.
Either way, do not miss the poetry.
Love is being described as fire.
Powerful.
Uncontainable.
Costly.

“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it...”
Song of Songs 8:7.
Biblical love is not sterile.
It burns.
But the Bible refuses to let the flame become god.
Love is powerful.
God is ultimate.
Desire is powerful.
God is Lord.
Sex is powerful.
God defines its purpose.
And Scripture's sexual ethic therefore makes sense only when we stop asking merely:
“What am I allowed to do?”
and start asking:
“What was my body created to say?”
Within the Bible's vision of marriage, sexual union is not merely recreation.
Genesis says the two become “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself returns to Genesis when speaking about marriage in Matthew 19.
And Paul later writes:
Ephesians 5:25.
Then, after quoting Genesis about the two becoming one flesh, Paul says:

“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Ephesians 5:32.
Be careful here.
Song of Songs should not be flattened into a code where every kiss, breast, garden, fragrance, or embrace secretly means something else.
It genuinely celebrates human love and desire.
Yet when the whole canon of Scripture is allowed to speak, marriage itself participates in a greater biblical mystery.
A faithful bridegroom loving his bride can point beyond himself.
Toward Christ.
Toward covenant.
Toward the Bridegroom who does not abandon His Bride.
Toward Jesus, who gave Himself for His people.
And suddenly “holy doesn't mean sexless” becomes only half the truth.
Holy means something far greater.
It means every part of you belongs to God.
Your mind.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your fantasies.
Your singleness.
Your marriage.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your desire.
Even the places you have been too ashamed to bring into prayer.
All of it.
Because Jesus is not asking for the religious version of you.
He wants you.
The person underneath the Sunday clothes.
The person underneath the worship songs.
The person underneath the browser history.
The person underneath the secret relationship.
The person underneath the memories.
The person underneath the shame.
Maybe you have never prayed honestly about your sexuality because you thought mentioning it to God would somehow shock Him.
He made you.
He already knows.
So stop giving Jesus edited prayers.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I'm lonely.”
“Lord, I want someone.”
“Lord, I'm tempted.”
“Lord, I miss being touched.”
“Lord, my marriage feels cold.”
“Lord, pornography has a grip on me.”
“Lord, I crossed a line.”
“Lord, I keep fantasizing.”
“Lord, I'm angry that I'm still single.”
“Lord, I don't understand these desires.”
“Lord, I want to be holy, but I am tired of pretending this battle isn't real.”
That prayer may be more sacred than a thousand polished religious sentences.
Because transformation begins in the light.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
No more hiding.
Not from Christ.
Confess your sins.
Seek wise, trustworthy Christian accountability where needed.
Remove access to what continually feeds your sin.
Stop calling bondage “just how I am.”
Stop calling temptation identity.
Stop calling compromise love.
Stop calling shame repentance.
And stop believing that your worst sexual failure is more powerful than the blood of Jesus Christ.
It isn't.
If you belong to Christ, your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not own your future.
This is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Jesus and became a preacher of Christ.
Paul persecuted the Church and became an apostle of the Gospel.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history, yet Jesus deliberately met her at the well and spoke to the thirst beneath the thirst.
Again and again, Scripture shows us a Savior who walks directly into human wreckage and starts rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin was beautiful.
By making redemption beautiful.
Maybe that is what Jesus is doing with you now.
Rewriting what lust wrote.
Rewriting what abuse wrote.
Rewriting what pornography wrote.
Rewriting what adultery wrote.
Rewriting what rejection wrote.
Rewriting what loneliness wrote.
Rewriting what your ex wrote.
Rewriting what your own choices wrote.
The scar may remain part of your testimony.
But the scar does not get to write the ending.
Jesus does.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only believer fighting this battle.
And if you know someone who has confused holiness with shame, send this to them.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating with your convictions.
Come back when your body is loud and obedience feels expensive.
Come back when shame tells you Jesus doesn't want you.
Help us keep putting Christ in front of them.
It cannot.
If you genuinely want your resources to glorify God, consider putting some of them behind work that proclaims His Word rather than only behind things that disappear.
If this ministry feeds you, help us feed someone else.
Not to prove you love Jesus.
Because you already know someone who needs to read it.
Someone ashamed of their desires.
Someone losing a private war with pornography.
Someone sleeping beside a spouse while feeling painfully alone.
Someone single and wondering why God gave them desires He has not yet allowed them to fulfill.
Someone convinced their sexual past disqualified them from being loved by God.
Someone who thinks holiness means becoming less human.
Tell them.
Holy doesn't mean sexless.
It means surrendered.
Desire doesn't have to disappear.
It has to learn where to kneel.
Your body is not your god.
Your sexuality is not your identity.
Your temptation is not your master.
Your past is not your name.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And when desire kneels before Him, grace begins teaching the heart how to burn without being consumed.
Remember this when the old shame comes whispering again:
The chapter you are most ashamed to let Jesus read may become the very page where He writes grace in the largest letters.
